stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.fps.lau.justification: The blueprint asserts the specific calculation: “The constant series 𝟙 = (1,1,1,…) … satisfies (1 − x) · 𝟙 = 0,” and then its nonzero consequences. The target concludes only `∃ p f, p ≠ 0 ∧ f ≠ 0 ∧ laurentPolynomialSmul p f = 0`; it neither fixes `p` to `1 - x` nor `f` to the constant-one family. Thus it formalizes existence of some torsion witnesses, not the stated example. The difference enters in the target’s existential binders `∃ p f`; these should be replaced or supplemented by the equation for the explicit Laurent polynomial `1-x` and series `fun _ : ℤ => 1`, together with their nonzeroness. There is also an added binder `[Nontrivial K]`. The section assumption says that `K` is a commutative ℚ-algebra, while the supplied definitions of commutative ring and algebra do not require `0 ≠ 1`; hence `[Nontrivial K]` is a mathematically contentful restriction not licensed by those definitions. Although replacing the ℚ-algebra setting by the more general `[CommRing K]` would otherwise be acceptable, restricting it further to `[Nontrivial K]` excludes the trivial algebra. Faithfulness would require either carrying nontriviality in the blueprint’s algebra/ring convention or stating the blueprint under its actual ℚ-algebra setting without this extra restriction.

The elaborated signature quantifies `∀ (k : ℕ)`, which matches “For all $k \ge 0$” by representing nonnegative indices as natural numbers. Its conclusion `2 * ∑ i ∈ Finset.range k, 3 ^ i < 3 ^ k` matches `$2 \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} 3^i < 3^k$`, since `Finset.range k` is documented as the natural numbers less than `k`. The referenced instances show that the sum, multiplication, powers, and inequality are interpreted in `ℤ`, which faithfully supports the stated integer-valued inequality and introduces no additional mathematical hypothesis.

The two declarations jointly state exactly the two coefficient shifts in the blueprint. `T_mul_coeff` quantifies over `(a : LaurentPolynomial K) (n : ℤ)` and proves `(LaurentPolynomial.T 1 * a) n = a (n - 1)`, matching “$T(1)\cdot a=(a_{n-1})_{n\in\mathbb Z}$.” Likewise, `T_neg_one_mul_coeff` proves `(LaurentPolynomial.T (-1) * a) n = a (n + 1)`, matching “$T(-1)\cdot a=(a_{n+1})_{n\in\mathbb Z}$.” Pointwise equality for every integer coefficient is precisely the asserted family equality. The binder `[CommRing K]` agrees with the blueprint’s commutative-ring setting, and Mathlib’s `LaurentPolynomial K` is a finitely supported function on `ℤ`, matching the informal definition of Laurent polynomials as essentially finite integer-indexed families.

The blueprint says that a Laurent series “equals the summable-family sum of the monomials $f_n\cdot x^n$,” with each monomial represented by $(\delta_{m,n}f_n)_{m\in\mathbb Z}$. The target asserts exactly `x = (AlgebraicCombinatorics.FPS.Laurent.singleFamily x).hsum`. By the body of `singleFamily`, its term at an index `g` in `HahnSeries.support x` is `(HahnSeries.single g) (x.coeff g)`, and `HahnSeries.single` is the series with coefficient `x.coeff g` at `g` and zero elsewhere, i.e. the stated monomial. Indexing the sum by the support merely omits zero monomials and still recovers the stated decomposition. The binder `[CommRing K]` supplies the coefficient setting needed for this construction; if the notation $K((x))$ was intended only for fields, the formal theorem is more general, not weaker.

The two declarations exactly cover the two clauses of the blueprint. `T_coeff_eq` quantifies `∀ {K} [CommRing K] (k i : ℤ)` and concludes `(LaurentPolynomial.T k) i = if i = k then 1 else 0`, which is precisely “for each k ∈ ℤ … T(k)ᵢ = δᵢ,ₖ.” `T_one_zpow` quantifies `∀ {K} [CommRing K] (k : ℤ)` and concludes `↑(⋯.unit ^ k) = LaurentPolynomial.T k`; the left side uses the bundled unit associated to `T 1`, so `^ k` is an integer power via `Units.instDivInvMonoid`, exactly matching “T(1)^k = T(k) … using integer powers via the unit structure.” The `[CommRing K]` binder is the coefficient-ring setting fixed by the informal definitions, not an added hypothesis.

The target exactly formalizes only the second sentence: its binders `∀ {K} [CommRing K] (f : PowerSeries K) (n : ℕ)` and equality `(powerSeriesToLaurent f).coeff ↑n = (PowerSeries.coeff n) f` match “For power series embedded into Laurent series, the coefficient at non-negative index n ∈ ℕ is preserved.” However, the INFORMAL STATEMENT also asserts: “For any k ∈ ℤ and n ∈ ℤ, the coefficient [x^n] T(k) equals δ_{n,k}.” The target has no binder `k : ℤ`, does not quantify over integer `n`, and contains neither `T` nor a Kronecker-delta conclusion. More decisively, no project or informal definition of `T(k)` is supplied, so this missing clause cannot be expressed from the available definitions. A definition/declaration of `T : ℤ → LaurentSeries K` (or its intended equivalent) is needed, after which a separate theorem or an expanded target asserting its coefficients are `1` at `n = k` and `0` otherwise would be required.

The blueprint fixes “a commutative ring K” and quantifies “for all k, i ∈ ℤ”; the elaborated signature has exactly `{K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K] (k i : ℤ)`. Its conclusion `↑(⋯.unit ^ k) i = if i = k then 1 else 0` states that the coefficient at index `i` of the integer power of the unit representing `x = T 1` is `1` precisely when `i = k`, and `0` otherwise. This right-hand side is exactly the informal definition of `δ_{i,k}`. Thus it faithfully formalizes the coefficient of `x^k` as the Kronecker delta.

To make the declaration faithful, either the blueprint must explicitly assume that `K` is a commutative ring, or these dependencies and the target must be generalized to the weaker algebraic setting intended by the blueprint, using ordered partial products if commutativity is unavailable.

The restriction enters because `Finset.prod` requires a `CommMonoid`, leading here to `CommRing K`. To make the formalization faithful without adding commutativity to the blueprint, use an ordered recursive/list partial product and weaken the coefficient structure accordingly (for example to `Ring K`, consistent with the supplied subtraction operation).

There are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers. The inclusion of `k` in `⟨k, ts⟩` merely represents the length-indexed tuple, including the empty case `k = 0`.

The blueprint requires a tuple “whose horizontal concatenation reproduces T.” The target codomain is only `(k : ℕ) × (Fin k → (m : ℕ) × { T' // DominoTilingsZ.isFaultfree m T' })`. Thus it certifies that every returned component is faultfree, but contains no condition relating the component widths or tilings back to the input `T`: there is no assertion that the widths sum to `n`, that the pieces occur in the required order, or that their horizontal concatenation equals `T`. The recursive body follows the described cutting algorithm, including the `n = 0`, faultfree, and minimum-fault cases, but it does not itself provide the missing reconstruction proposition in the declaration’s result type. This is expressible using a reconstruction/concatenation predicate built from the available tiling, domino-set, and shift notions. To make the declaration faithful, define such a predicate (for example `ConcatenatesTo n T ts`) and return a subtype carrying a proof of it, such as `(k : ℕ) × { ts : Fin k → (m : ℕ) × {T' // isFaultfree m T'} // ConcatenatesTo n T ts }`, or provide a theorem asserting that `decomposeTiling n T` satisfies that predicate.

The target quantifies over exactly the intended data, `∀ (n : ℕ) (T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2))`, and concludes that after `decomposeTiling n T = ⟨k, ts⟩`, `∑ i, (ts i).fst = n`. By the dependency signature, each `ts i` has type `(m : ℕ) × { T' // isFaultfree m T'}`, so `(ts i).fst` is precisely the component width `m_i`; and `i : Fin k` ranges over all returned components. Thus the formal equality is exactly the blueprint’s `∑ᵢ m_i = n`, with no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The target quantifies over exactly the stated data, `∀ {n : ℕ} {T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2)} {k : ℕ}`, assumes `hasFault n T k`, and concludes for every `d ∈ T.dominos` that `d.inLeftPart k ∨ d.inRightPart k`. The conclusion definitions exactly match the blueprint’s parentheticals: `inLeftPart` means `∀ p ∈ d.toShape, p.1 ≤ ↑k`, while `inRightPart` means `∀ p ∈ d.toShape, p.1 ≥ ↑k + 1`. The body of `hasFault` expresses an internal fault (`k > 0 ∧ k < n`) where a horizontal domino starts strictly left of `k` or at least at `k+1`; vertical dominos cannot straddle a vertical fault line. Thus it formalizes “At a fault position k ... each domino ... lies entirely in the left part ... or ... the right part,” with no additional hypotheses.

The hypothesis binder `hk : DominoTilingsZ.hasFault n T k` directly formalizes “At a fault position k,” for a tiling `T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2)`. The conclusion states exactly that `T.dominos` is the union of `(restrictTilingLeft n T k hk).dominos` and the image of the right restriction under `fun d => d.shiftNat k`. This matches “the left restriction’s dominos and the right restriction’s dominos shifted back by k.” In particular, `restrictTilingRight` first shifts right-part dominos by `-k` via `shiftNeg k`, while `shiftNat k` shifts them by `+k`, so the conclusion restores those dominos to their positions in the original tiling. There are no additional theorem hypotheses beyond the fault premise and the setting needed by the restriction definitions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.f.justification: The formal binders exactly match the blueprint hypotheses: `∀ n ≥ 2`, a tiling `T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2)`, and membership `Domino.vertical 1 1 ∈ T.dominos`. By `Domino.toShape`, `Domino.vertical 1 1` covers `{(1,1), (1,2)}`, exactly the informal vertical domino. The conclusion `hasFault n T 1` unfolds to `1 > 0 ∧ 1 < n ∧ ∀ d ∈ T.dominos, ...`; the first two conditions follow from the position and `n ≥ 2`, while its horizontal-domino clause `i < 1 ∨ i ≥ 1 + 1` says precisely that no horizontal domino straddles the line between columns 1 and 2. Thus it formalizes “T has a fault at position 1” with no additional mathematical hypotheses.

The binders exactly match the blueprint hypotheses: `∀ n ≥ 3` formalizes “If n ≥ 3,” and `∀ (T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2))` formalizes “the tiling T of R_{n,2}.” The premise `Domino.horizontal 1 1 ∈ T.dominos` denotes the domino whose `toShape` is `{(1,1), (1 + 1,1)} = {(1,1),(2,1)}`, exactly the stated horizontal domino. The conclusion `hasFault n T 2` says `2 > 0 ∧ 2 < n` and that every horizontal domino starts either before column 2 or at least at column 3, hence none starts at column 2 and straddles the vertical line after column 2. This is precisely a fault at position 2. The formal `Rectangle`, `Tiling`, and `Domino.toShape` bodies agree with the supplied informal definitions, and there are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The target states `∀ (n : ℕ) (T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2)), isFaultfree n T → n = 1 ∨ n = 2`, which matches the classification’s quantifier and conclusion. However, the blueprint package never defines “faultfree.” The formal dependency defines it as `n > 0 ∧ ∀ (k : ℕ), ¬ hasFault n T k`, with `hasFault` restricted by `k > 0 ∧ k < n` and a specific no-horizontal-domino-straddles condition. In particular, the added conjunct `n > 0` could materially exclude the width-zero rectangle rather than merely encode notation. Without an informal definition of “fault” and “faultfree,” it is impossible to determine whether these conditions capture the blueprint term. The package would need the blueprint’s definition of faultfree tilings, including whether nonemptiness is required and which boundary lines count as faults.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.h.justification: The target quantifies `∀ n ≥ 1` whereas the blueprint assumes a tiling of `R_{n,2}` “with `n ≥ 2`.” This is strictly more general: every `n ≥ 2` satisfies the formal theorem’s weaker bound `n ≥ 1`. The remaining content matches exactly: `T : Tiling (Rectangle n 2)` formalizes a tiling of `R_{n,2}`, and `Domino.horizontal 1 1` and `Domino.horizontal 1 2` have shapes `{(1,1),(2,1)}` and `{(1,2),(2,2)}` by `Domino.toShape`. Thus the formal implication proves the blueprint statement, with a harmlessly wider range of `n`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.n.justification: The elaborated signature is exactly “∀ (n : ℕ), d_[n,2] = Nat.fib (n + 1),” matching “For any n ∈ ℕ, d_{n,2} = f_{n+1}.” Here `d_[n,2]` unfolds to `Nat.card (Tiling (Rectangle n 2))`, the defined number of domino tilings of the n×2 rectangle. `Nat.fib` satisfies `fib 0 = 0`, `fib 1 = 1`, and `fib (n + 2) = fib n + fib (n + 1)`, which is the same Fibonacci sequence as the informal definition. There are no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

The blueprint states, “For any $n \in \mathbb N$, $d_{n+2,2}=d_{n,2}+d_{n+1,2}$.” The elaborated signature is exactly `∀ (n : ℕ), d_[n + 2,2] = d_[n,2] + d_[n + 1,2]`, with no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers. Moreover, `numTilings` is defined as `fun n m => Nat.card (Tiling (Rectangle n m))`, matching the intended number of domino tilings of the `n × m` rectangle.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.p.justification: The blueprint says: “For any weighted set $A$ and any $n\in\mathbb N$, there is a canonical isomorphism of weighted sets $A^{n+1}\cong A\times A^n$.” The elaborated signature quantifies over exactly these data, `{α : Type u_2} → (W : WeightedSet α) → (n : ℕ)`, with no added hypotheses, and returns `(W.pow (n + 1)).Isomorphism (W ×ᵥ W.pow n)`. By the dependency bodies, `W.pow k` has carrier `Fin k → α` and weight `∑ i, W.weight (f i)`, matching the weighted Cartesian power, while `WeightedSet.prod` uses the sum of component weights. `WeightedSet.Isomorphism` is precisely a weight-preserving bijection. The body supplies the canonical coordinate decomposition: `Fin.succFunEquiv` identifies an `(n+1)`-tuple with an `n`-tuple and one element, and `Equiv.prodComm` reorders this to `α × (Fin n → α)`. Thus the formal definition constructs exactly the claimed canonical weighted-set isomorphism.

The target quantifies exactly over “Given a tiling T of R_{m,2}” via `(m : ℕ) → Tiling (Rectangle m 2)` and returns a tiling of the required rectangle via `Tiling (Rectangle (m + 2) 2)`. Its body gives the asserted domino set exactly: `{horizontal 1 1, horizontal 1 2} ∪ (fun d => d.shiftNat 2) '' T.dominos`. By `Domino.toShape`, these two constructors cover `{(1,1),(2,1)}` and `{(1,2),(2,2)}`; by `shiftNat` and `shift`, every old domino is shifted horizontally right by 2. Finally, constructing `Tiling` includes proofs of pairwise disjointness and that the union equals the rectangle, so “gives a valid tiling” is fully represented. There are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The blueprint says: “Given a tiling T of R_{m,2}, prepending a vertical domino {(1,1),(1,2)} and shifting all of T’s dominos right by 1 gives a valid tiling of R_{m+1,2}.” The elaborated signature quantifies over every `m : ℕ` and every `T : DominoTilingsZ.Tiling (DominoTilingsZ.Rectangle m 2)`, returning `DominoTilingsZ.Tiling (DominoTilingsZ.Rectangle (m + 1) 2)`, with no added hypotheses. Its body sets `dominos := {DominoTilingsZ.Domino.vertical 1 1} ∪ (fun d => d.shiftNat 1) '' T.dominos`. By `Domino.vertical` and `Domino.toShape`, the new domino covers exactly `{(1,1),(1,2)}`; by `shiftNat` and `shift`, every old domino is shifted horizontally right by 1. The `Tiling` constructor’s disjointness and cover fields certify that this exact set is a valid tiling of the target rectangle. Thus the formal declaration matches the informal statement.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.r.justification: The target exactly returns a tiling of `Rectangle k 2` whose dominos are `{d | d ∈ T.dominos ∧ d.inLeftPart k}`, matching “the set of dominos lying in the left part forms a valid tiling of `R_{k,2}`.” However, its hypothesis is specifically `hk : DominoTilingsZ.hasFault n T k`, whose body adds `k > 0 ∧ k < n` and a particular no-straddling condition. The blueprint package provides no INFORMAL DEFINITION of “a fault at position k,” so it is unavailable whether faults are required to be strictly internal or whether positions such as `k = 0` or `k = n` count. Thus the package cannot determine whether the binders `k > 0` and `k < n` are legitimate parts of the notion or added restrictions. An informal definition of “fault at position k” (and ideally “left part”) is needed. If it agrees with `hasFault` and `Domino.inLeftPart`, the declaration is faithful; otherwise `hasFault` would need to be changed to match that definition.

The blueprint says, “For $k \ge 2$, the left restriction of the composed tiling at the first boundary $m_1$ equals the first component’s tiling.” The formal binders match this setting: `∀ (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≥ 2) (ts : Fin k → (m : ℕ) × { T' // ... isFaultfree m T' })`, and the equality restricts `composeTilings k ts` at `(ts ⟨0, ⋯⟩).fst`, exactly the first width, with right-hand side `↑(ts ⟨0, ⋯⟩).snd`, exactly the first tiling. The binder `hfault : hasFault ... (ts ⟨0, ⋯⟩).fst` is not a contentful added restriction: `restrictTilingLeft` requires a proof that its cut position is a fault. In this setting that fact is inherent in the first boundary of a composition of at least two faultfree, positive-width components (`isFaultfree m T'` includes `m > 0`), so `hfault` supplies the dependent proof needed to form the restriction rather than narrowing the mathematical claim.

The formal binders exactly encode that `k` is the minimum fault: `hk : DominoTilingsZ.hasFault n T k` says that `k` is a fault, while `(∀ j < k, ¬ DominoTilingsZ.hasFault n T j)` says that no smaller position is a fault. The conclusion `DominoTilingsZ.isFaultfree k (DominoTilingsZ.restrictTilingLeft n T k hk)` directly states that the left restriction is faultfree. Although `isFaultfree` quantifies over every natural fault position, `hasFault k ... j` itself includes `j < k`, so positions outside the restricted rectangle's interior are automatically not faults. Its additional conjunct `k > 0` is already supplied by `hk`, since `hasFault n T k` includes `k > 0`. Thus this faithfully formalizes: “The left restriction at the minimum fault position is faultfree.”

The blueprint assumes only “a fault at position $k$,” described as a vertical line that no domino straddles; it does not restrict $k$ to an interior position. However, the target’s binder `hk : DominoTilingsZ.hasFault n T k` unfolds to the additional hypotheses `k > 0 ∧ k < n ∧ ...`. These make the declaration weaker by excluding the boundary positions `k = 0` and `k = n`, even though the stated restriction-and-shift construction is meaningful there. The discrepancy enters through the body of `DominoTilingsZ.hasFault`, not through `restrictTilingRight` itself. To match the statement as given, `hasFault` should express only the no-straddling condition, or the target should accept that condition directly; alternatively, the informal statement would need to specify `0 < k < n`. The conclusion itself is accurate: the returned tiling has domino set `(fun d => d.shiftNeg k) '' {d | d ∈ T.dominos ∧ d.inRightPart k}` and shape `Rectangle (n - k) 2`.

The blueprint states: “For $k \ge 2$, the right restriction of the composed tiling at the first boundary $m_1$, after shifting, equals the composition of the tail $(t_2,\ldots,t_k)$.” The formal binders match this setting: `∀ (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≥ 2) (ts : Fin k → (m : ℕ) × { T' // isFaultfree m T' })`, and its conclusion identifies `restrictTilingRight ... (ts ⟨0, ⋯⟩).fst` with `composeTilings (k - 1) (faultfreeTilingsTail k ⋯ ts)`, up to the necessary transport `⋯ ▸` arising from equality of rectangle widths. The `hfault : hasFault ... (ts ⟨0, ⋯⟩).fst` binder supplies the dependent proof required by `restrictTilingRight`; it encodes that the stated first boundary is a valid fault position rather than changing the mathematical equality. This is carried by the setting: each component is faultfree and has positive width by `isFaultfree`, and `composeTilings` concatenates the components, making their boundary a fault. Thus the declaration faithfully formalizes the stated right restriction and tail composition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.t.justification: The blueprint says: “For any $n,m\in\mathbb N$, the set of all domino tilings of $R_{n,m}$ is finite.” The target has exactly the corresponding quantifiers, `∀ (n m : ℕ)`, and asserts `Set.univ.Finite`, i.e. finiteness of the universal set of elements of the tiling type for the rectangle. The referenced definitions match the blueprint: `Rectangle n m` is `{(i,j) | 1 ≤ i ≤ n ∧ 1 ≤ j ≤ m}`, and `Tiling S` consists of pairwise-disjoint dominos whose union is `S`. Thus the universal set is precisely the set of all domino tilings of `R_{n,m}`. There are no added hypotheses or restricted ranges.

The elaborated signature, `∀ {α : Type u_2} (W : WeightedSet α), W.IsFiniteType → W.HasPositiveWeights → W.tuples.IsFiniteType`, exactly matches: “Let A be a finite-type weighted set such that every element has weight ≥ 1 ... Then ... all finite tuples ... is also a finite-type weighted set.” The dependency bodies preserve each meaning: `IsFiniteType` is `∀ n, {a | W.weight a = n}.Finite`; `HasPositiveWeights` is `∀ a, W.weight a ≥ 1`; and `tuples` has carrier `(n : ℕ) × (Fin n → α)` with weight `∑ i, W.weight (f i)`, which represents the disjoint union of all finite powers, including the unique empty tuple at `n = 0`. There are no additional mathematically contentful hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf-ws.w.justification: The target states exactly `FaultfreeTilingsHeight2.weightGenFun ... = PowerSeries.X + PowerSeries.X ^ 2`, matching the blueprint’s “weight generating function of faultfree height-2 tilings is x + x².” By definition, `FaultfreeTilingsHeight2` consists of dependent pairs `((n : ℕ) × {T // isFaultfree n T})` and has weight `n`, so its coefficients count faultfree tilings by rectangle width. `WeightedSet.weightGenFun` constructs the formal power series whose nth coefficient is precisely `W.countOfWeight hft n`. The supplied `faultfreeTilingsHeight2_isFiniteType` argument is only the finiteness witness needed to define those coefficients, not an added hypothesis or restriction. Finally, `PowerSeries.X` has the stipulated meaning of the FPS variable x, so the right side is exactly x + x².

The blueprint says “The weight generating function of $D$ equals $\sum_n f_{n+1}x^n$,” but the package contains no INFORMAL DEFINITION identifying $D$. The formal side instead fixes the object through `DominoTilingsZ.TilingsHeight2`, whose body is the weighted set `((n : ℕ) × Tiling (Rectangle n 2))` with weight `n`. Although the target’s right-hand side, `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(Nat.fib (n + 1))`, matches the stated Fibonacci coefficients, the package does not establish that informal $D$ denotes this weighted set. An informal definition of $D$—and, if relevant, the coefficient ring of its generating function—is needed to decide faithfulness.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf.deri.justification: The blueprint states the identity for FPSs over an arbitrary field: the geometric-series definition says “$(1-x)^{-1}\in K[[x]]$ (where $K$ is a field),” and the derivative definition likewise uses coefficients in $K$. The target instead fixes the coefficient field to the rationals throughout: `PowerSeries.derivative ℚ` and hence `(1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ : PowerSeries ℚ`. This narrows the implicit quantification over fields and therefore proves only a special case. To be faithful, the target should introduce a binder such as `{K : Type*} [Field K]` and state `(PowerSeries.derivative K) (1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ = (1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ ^ 2` over `PowerSeries K`. Apart from this restriction, the formal derivative and formal-power-series inverse match the blueprint definitions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf.geom.justification: The blueprint defines the identity in `K[[x]]`, explicitly “where `K` is a field,” so the statement ranges over an arbitrary coefficient field `K`. The elaborated target has no binders at all: `(1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ = PowerSeries.mk fun x => 1`. The listed elaboration dependencies (`Rat.instField`, `Rat.addGroup`, `Rat.semiring`, and `Rat.instOfNat`) show that this is a theorem only about `PowerSeries ℚ`. Thus the coefficient field has been narrowed from arbitrary `K` to `ℚ`, making the formal theorem weaker. The series on the right is otherwise correct: `PowerSeries.mk fun x => 1` is the FPS with every coefficient equal to one, i.e. `∑_{n≥0} x^n`. To make the declaration faithful, add binders such as `{K : Type*} [Field K]` and state the equality in `PowerSeries K` (with any necessary type annotations).

The binder `∀ (α : ℚ)` exactly matches “For any α ∈ ℚ.” The equality is in `PowerSeries ℚ`: `PowerSeries.X` is the formal variable x, and `PowerSeries.mk fun n => α ^ n` is the FPS whose n-th coefficient is αⁿ, hence represents `∑_{n≥0} α^n x^n` under the supplied FPS and generating-function definitions. The left side `(1 - α • PowerSeries.X)⁻¹` represents `1/(1-αx)`. There are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers; the denominator has constant coefficient 1, so it is invertible as required by the blueprint’s fraction notation.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf.sum_.justification: The blueprint states the FPS identity using a general coefficient field: its definitions use `K[[x]]`, and the geometric-series definition explicitly says “where `K` is a field.” The target has no coefficient-type binder at all: `(PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑n + 1) = (1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ ^ 2`, and the elaboration references `Rat.instNatCast`, `Rat.instField`, and related instances, so this is only an equality in `PowerSeries ℚ`. Restricting the coefficient field from arbitrary `K` with `[Field K]` to `ℚ` narrows the blueprint’s quantification and is therefore weaker. The difference enters in the target’s missing `{K : Type*} [Field K]` binders. It would be faithful if generalized to those binders, with the coefficient explicitly interpreted in `K`, e.g. `PowerSeries.mk (fun n => (n : K) + 1) = (1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ ^ 2`.

The blueprint states the FPS identity using the generic coefficient field from its definitions: “the geometric series is … $(1-x)^{-1}\in K[[x]]$ (where $K$ is a field).” The elaborated target has no coefficient-type binder and instead asserts only the equality in `PowerSeries ℚ`, as shown by `↑n` resolving through `Rat.instNatCast` and inversion through `Rat.instField`. Thus it narrows the generic field $K$ to the single field `ℚ`, making the formal theorem weaker than the blueprint. The representation `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑n` correctly encodes $\sum_{n\ge 0} n x^n$. To be faithful, the target should quantify over a coefficient type, e.g. `{K : Type*} [Field K]`, and state `(PowerSeries.mk fun n => (n : K)) = PowerSeries.X * (1 - PowerSeries.X)⁻¹ ^ 2`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.gf.weig.justification: The target faithfully captures only the decomposition-isomorphism portion: `DominoTilingsZ.TilingsHeight2.Isomorphism DominoTilingsZ.FaultfreeTilingsHeight2.tuples`, with `toFun := ... decomposeTiling`, inverse `composeTilings`, and `weight_eq`, expresses a unique weight-preserving bijection with finite tuples, including the 0-tuple and 1-tuple cases implemented by `decomposeTiling._unary`. However, the INFORMAL STATEMENT also asserts the generating-function conclusions `\overline D = \overline{F^0+F^1+\cdots}` and `= 1/(1-\overline F)`. No project definition in the package provides finite-type weighted sets, weight generating functions, formal power series, infinite sums, or the geometric-series expression, so these clauses cannot be stated using the available formal definitions. To make the complete blueprint statement statable and faithful, the project dependencies would need formal definitions of finite-type and `\overline A`, the tuple/disjoint-union generating-function theorem, and the geometric-series identity; the target would then need to include those equalities or be accompanied by formal corollaries deriving them. As supplied, it is a faithful formalization of the first part but the complete INFORMAL STATEMENT is unstatable.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.imagefi.justification: The target quantifies over exactly the relevant data, `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (P : Finset (Fin n))`, and asserts `imageFinset σ Pᶜ = (imageFinset σ P)ᶜ`. By the dependency body, `imageFinset σ P` is `Finset.map` under the bijection `σ`, hence is precisely the informal image `{σ(i) | i ∈ P}`. The `Finset` complement is taken in the finite ambient type `Fin n`, matching complement inside `[n]`. Thus the equality is exactly “σ(\overline P) = \overline{σ(P)}.” Although the informal convention defines `[n]` for integer `n` while Lean uses `n : ℕ` and represents the n-element set as `Fin n` rather than `{1,…,n}`, this causes no mathematical loss: positive cases differ only by relabeling, and every nonpositive informal `[n]` is empty and is represented by `Fin 0`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.jtp.coe.justification: The target quantifies exactly as required: `∀ (d : ℕ)`, matching “For each d ∈ ℕ,” and applies `PowerSeries.coeff d` to both sides, matching `[q^d]`. On the left, it sums over `Finset ℕ × Finset ℕ`, the formal encoding of pairs of finite subsets `(P,N)`. By the dependency bodies, `jacobiFactorZ n - 1` is `q^(2*n+1) z` and `jacobiFactorZInv n - 1` is `q^(2*n+1) z⁻¹`, so the two finite products match the displayed products. On the right, `stateGenFun` sums over `pair : ℤ × (n : ℕ) × n.Partition`; this is precisely an integer ℓ together with a partition μ of size n. Its summand is `stateMonomial (ℓ.natAbs ^ 2 + 2 * n) ℓ`, which expands to `q^(ℓ²+2|μ|) z^ℓ`. Thus the formal equality is the coefficient identity stated in the blueprint, with no additional hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

The blueprint defines the pentagonal series generically as “Q = … ∈ R[[x]]”, whereas the target quantifies only `∀ (n : ℕ)` and fixes the coefficient ring through `PowerSeries.derivative ℤ` (and consequently specializes `pentagonalSeries` and the coefficient equality to `ℤ`). Thus it proves only the integer-coefficient instance, not the statement over the arbitrary ring `R` fixed by the informal definition. This is a restricted quantifier/setting, even though the dependency `pentagonalSeries` itself supports `{R : Type u_1} → [CommRing R] → PowerSeries R`. To make it faithful, generalize the target to bind `{R : Type*} [CommRing R]`, use `PowerSeries.derivative R`, instantiate `pentagonalSeries` over `R`, and cast `(-1) ^ k.natAbs` and `n` into `R` on the right-hand side. Apart from this specialization, the match on `pentagonalNumberInverse n` expresses the blueprint’s two cases.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.jtp.dou.justification: The target quantifies over exactly the required finite subsets, `∀ (P N : Finset ℕ)`, matching the informal products over finite sets `P` and `N`. By the dependency bodies, `jacobiFactorZ n - 1 = (1 + PowerSeries.X^(2*n+1) * jacobiZ) - 1`, hence represents `q^(2n+1) z`, and similarly `jacobiFactorZInv n - 1` represents `q^(2n+1) z⁻¹`. The right side `PowerSeries.X ^ (∑ n ∈ P, (2*n+1) + ∑ n ∈ N, (2*n+1)) * jacobiZPow (↑P.card - ↑N.card)` exactly formalizes `q^{∑_{n∈P}(2n+1)+∑_{n∈N}(2n+1)} · z^{|P|-|N|}`; in particular, the casts make the cardinality difference an integer, as required for a Laurent power of `z`. The fixed ambient ring `PowerSeries (LaurentPolynomial ℤ)` is also precisely the stated `([1mℤ[0m[z^{±}])[[q]]` setting.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.jtp.ene.justification: The target states `∀ (S : AlgebraicCombinatorics.State), ∃ n, S.energy = S.parnum.natAbs ^ 2 + 2 * n`. Here `n : ℕ`, forced by the natural-valued expression (`S.energy : ℕ` and `S.parnum.natAbs : ℕ`), so the informal condition “there exists `n ≥ 0`” is encoded exactly by quantification over naturals. `Int.natAbs` represents `|parnum(S)|`, and the supplied definitions of `energy` and `parnum` implement the half-integer conventions from the informal definition. The displayed equality is therefore exactly `energy(S) = |parnum(S)|² + 2n`. It also implies the stated consequences: the energy is at least the square and its excess is even.
